title: OPINION: Ghosts probably aren't real. The scary ones, anyway
site_name: OPINION: Ghosts probably aren't real. The scary ones, anyway - Indiana Daily Student
excerpt: You may have seen a ghost. Science suggests nobody was there with you.
content:
Editor's note: All opinions, columns and letters reflect the views of the individual writer and not necessarily those of the IDS or its staffers. 

Have you ever been approached by a woman in a veil, dressed in black, on a dark October night? Has she ever followed you home along Third Street or hurled rocks in your direction? Did she happen to float above the ground or pass through solid objects?  

If you answered yes to any of these questions, you may have encountered the Woman in Black — the subject of an Indiana University ghost story with an account that first appeared in your own Indiana Daily Student’s Oct. 9, 1911, newspaper. At one point in time, Third Street’s notorious haunt was apparently so terrifying that she inspired a student to take up arms in self-defense.  

Belief in the paranormal, like the story of the Woman in Black, isn’t as uncommon as many people think. A 2025 Gallup poll showed 39% of Americans believe in ghosts.  

That number seems high for a phenomenon which, at least so far, lacks any kind of scientific evidence to support it. But then again, if ghosts are completely imaginary, why do so many people report seeing, hearing or feeling them?  

People clearly believe these supposed spiritual encounters are real, even if the ghosts themselves might not be. But that doesn’t make our experiences with them any less meaningful, or any less worth understanding.  

One type of ghost you can probably stop worrying about is the kind that moves things, like IU’s Woman in Black. How can a body that can pass through walls be solid enough to lift a book off a shelf, or huck a rock at an unsuspecting student? Ghosts like these would have to be made of something both intangible and solid at the same time — and nothing in the observable universe we’ve found so far can do that.  

Even with spirits that don’t manipulate the physical world, other explanations often exist for the ghouls we glimpse out of the corner of our eyes or merely feel in the room. Haunted houses, for example, might be prone to ghost sightings partly because we expect them to be there.  

In 2000, psychologist Richard Wiseman and a team of English researchers set out to determine how the suggestion of a haunted area might influence what people report seeing there. To do so, they gathered 462 participants in Hampton Court Palace and told some of the group that an area of the palace had recently been associated with unusual phenomena. Then, the visitors were allowed to walk around and report what they found.  

The study revealed that visitors who already believed in ghosts and were told to expect strange activity reported more strange experiences — in other words, our minds have more to do with creating ghosts than simply noticing them.  

An even stranger example of the brain generating something that isn’t there is phantom limb syndrome, when a person who has undergone an amputation can still feel burning, tingling or itching sensations in a limb that is no longer there. Around 80% of amputees will experience phantom limb pain in their lifetimes. If the brain can generate the feeling of a hand where there isn’t one, it’s reasonable to believe it can generate a presence, too.  

In fact, in particularly dire situations, our brains may do just that. 

When Ernest Shackleton crossed the mountains of South Georgia Island in the southern Atlantic Ocean with two other members of his stranded Antarctic expedition in 1916, he later wrote that he felt the presence of an unknown fourth person trekking alongside them. Other explorers, climbers and disaster survivors have often described the same thing — an imaginary presence suddenly felt, rather than seen, bringing the person comfort in a life-or-death situation.   

That comfort is often overlooked when we think about ghosts. One study conducted on Welsh widows in 1971 found that almost half of the 293 people interviewed had sensed the presence of their departed loved one after their death. Furthermore, the majority of those who had these encounters said they found them helpful for grieving the person. The ghost stories we hear don’t usually have these happy endings, but maybe they should.  

So, next time you’re walking down Third Street and feel something watching you, don’t be so quick to assume it’s the Woman in Black. The scariest ghosts can usually be explained by what our own minds create out of expectation and fear, and the comforting ghosts don’t need to be real to matter to you. 

Spencer Schaberg (he/him) is a junior studying microbiology.
